briefOverview: Simeon reflects on his guilt in Joseph’s sale and uses Joseph’s merciful response as a warning against envy. The chapter broadens into moral exhortations and a brief prophecy about Simeon’s descendants’ future troubles.
summary: Simeon explains that his sadness comes from guilt over participating in the selling of Joseph, and he interprets his later binding in Egypt as just suffering. He praises Joseph as a Spirit-filled man who showed compassion and refused to hold malice, instead loving and enriching his brothers. Simeon therefore exhorts his children to reject jealousy and envy, to love one another sincerely, and to pursue integrity before God and people. He describes envy as spiritually and physically destructive, stirring anger, violence, inner turmoil, and even disturbing sleep. He then warns against fornication as a root of evils that separates from God and draws one toward “Beliar.” Finally, he cites a supposed writing of Enoch to predict future corruption and conflict involving Simeon’s descendants and Levi, ending with the claim that Simeon’s line will be few and lack sovereignty, in line with Jacob’s blessings.
externalContext: The “Testament of Simeon” is part of the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, a Jewish work (later transmitted in Christian circles) that presents the patriarchs giving ethical exhortations and predictions to their children. Its moral instruction—especially warnings against vices like envy and sexual immorality—resembles wisdom and penitential teaching common in Second Temple Judaism. The figure “Beliar” (Belial) appears in Jewish literature of this period as a name for a chief evil power, especially in sectarian writings such as those from Qumran.
externalReferences: Simeon’s confession and Joseph’s mercy point back to the Genesis narrative where Joseph is sold by his brothers (Genesis 37:18–28) and later recognizes and tests them in Egypt, including Simeon being bound (Genesis 42:18–24). The call to “make your hearts good… and your ways straight” echoes a biblical motif of finding favor with both God and people (cf. Proverbs 3:3–4). The prediction of Simeon’s diminished standing aligns with Jacob’s pronouncement that Simeon (with Levi) would be scattered in Israel (Genesis 49:5–7).
practicalQuestions: Where do jealousy or envy show up in my relationships, and what specific practices would help me “walk in singleness of heart” toward others?
How might Simeon’s acceptance of “just suffering” reshape the way I respond to consequences of my own wrong choices?
What does it look like, concretely, to love a sibling or peer “with a good heart” when trust has been damaged?
What patterns of thought (including at night or in private) reveal “malicious jealousy,” and what boundaries or habits could interrupt them?
If sexual behavior is portrayed here as spiritually corrosive, what safeguards (community, accountability, media choices) would make my “ways straight before men”?
uncertainAreas: The chapter’s appeal to a “writing of Enoch” is difficult to correlate with extant 1 Enoch passages with certainty; it may reflect a lost tradition or a generalized attribution. The specific historical referent of “harm to the sons of Levi with the sword” is not explicit in the text and could be symbolic, intra-tribal, or a retrospective interpretation by the author/redactor.
